overview:
Brazil is the largest country in South America and the fifth largest in the world, covering about 8.5 million km², nearly half the continent. It shares borders with every South American country except Chile and Ecuador, and its Atlantic coastline runs for more than 7,000 kilometers. Around 215 million people live there, more than in any other country in the Southern Hemisphere.

Brazil is the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas, a result of its history as a Portuguese colony. Its people are a rich blend of Indigenous, African, European, Middle Eastern and Japanese heritage, and most live in big coastal cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Salvador. The capital, Brasília, was built from scratch in the late 1950s in the empty center of the country and laid out in the shape of an airplane.

Brazil is a federal republic with an elected president and 26 states. It is a giant producer of coffee, soybeans, beef, iron ore and oil, and its soccer teams, music and Carnival are famous around the world.
landAndNature:
The Amazon rainforest covers about 60 percent of Brazil, the biggest rainforest on Earth, and the Amazon River pours more water into the sea than any other river. Farther south, the Pantanal is the world's largest wetland, where jaguars, capybaras, giant otters and caimans are easy to spot in the dry season. The Cerrado grasslands, the dry Northeast interior called the sertão, and the green Atlantic Forest along the coast each have their own plants and animals.

Brazil holds more species than any other country: pink river dolphins, toucans, sloths, howler monkeys, anacondas, piranhas and thousands of kinds of butterflies. Iguaçu Falls, on the Argentine border, sends about 275 waterfalls crashing into a jungle gorge. The climate is mostly tropical, with a cooler, frostier south.
peopleAndCulture:
Brazilian Portuguese has a musical sound and words borrowed from Indigenous Tupi and African languages. Rio's Carnival, the world's biggest party, fills the streets with samba schools, drums and towering floats in the days before Lent. Music styles born here include samba, bossa nova, forró and funk carioca, and capoeira blends martial art, dance and music.

Soccer is everywhere, from beach games to the national team, which has won the World Cup a record five times; Pelé is honored as the greatest player of all time. Favorite foods include feijoada, a black bean and pork stew; pão de queijo, chewy cheese bread; açaí berry bowls; and brigadeiros, chocolate fudge balls served at every birthday party. Religion is mostly Catholic, with strong Afro-Brazilian traditions such as Candomblé, especially in Bahia.
history:
Millions of Indigenous people lived across Brazil when the Portuguese navigator Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in 1500. Portugal set up sugar plantations and brought nearly five million enslaved Africans to work them, more than any other country in the Americas; slavery was not abolished until 1888, the last in the region to end it.

In 1808 the Portuguese royal family fled Napoleon and made Rio de Janeiro the capital of their empire. In 1822 Prince Pedro declared Brazil an independent empire with himself as emperor. Brazil became a republic in 1889 and grew rich on coffee. The 1900s brought waves of immigrants, the building of Brasília, and a military dictatorship from 1964 to 1985 that jailed and tortured opponents. Democracy returned in 1985, and a new constitution was adopted in 1988.
funFacts: The Amazon River carries about a fifth of all the fresh water that flows into the world's oceans.
Brasília was built in just 41 months, and its plan, seen from above, looks like an airplane or a bird.
Brazil is named after brazilwood, a tree whose red sap was used to dye cloth in Europe.
Brazil has the largest Japanese community outside Japan, centered in São Paulo.
Ilha da Queimada Grande, off the coast, has so many venomous golden lancehead snakes that visiting is banned.
The Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio stands 30 meters tall and is struck by lightning several times a year.
